q: How do you say the w in Wasser?
why: German w always sounds like English v.

q: Which syllable carries the stress in Entschuldigung?
why: ent- is never stressed, so the stress falls on the next syllable: ehnt-SHOOL-dih-goong.

q: How many syllables does Bitte have?
o: One: the final e is silent
Two: the final e is said, BIT-uh
why: A final e is always pronounced in German, like the a in about.

q: Which one asks a stranger's name?
why: Sie with a capital S is the polite you. With a small s, Wie heißen sie? asks what THEY are called.

q: Someone says Danke. What do you answer?
why: bitte means please, and it is also the answer to danke: you're welcome.

q: Your new friend at a party asks where you are from. What did they say?
why: Among friends people use du, and the verb with du ends in -st: kommst.

q: Why is it das Mädchen, although a girl is female?
o: Every noun ending in -chen is neuter
It is an old mistake that stuck
why: -chen always makes a noun neuter: grammar follows the ending, not the meaning.

q: Which article do plural nouns take?
why: In the plural every noun takes die: die Tage, die Frauen, die Bücher.

q: What is the best way to learn the word Tisch (table)?
o: With an English article: the Tisch
Guess the gender from the meaning
why: Gender cannot be guessed from the meaning, so learn the article and the noun together.

q: How do you say I'm a doctor? (a woman speaking)
why: No article before a job, and a woman uses the -in form: Ich bin Ärztin.

q: Which form of haben goes with Sie (formal you)?
why: Sie always shares the form of sie (they): Sie haben.

q: How do you usually say I'm hungry?
why: German says I have hunger: Ich habe Hunger.

q: Which sentence is right?
why: er takes -t: Er wohnt in Köln.

q: How do you say I'm working? (right now)
why: German has no -ing form: Ich arbeite covers I work and I'm working.

q: What can Sie kommen aus Kanada mean?
o: They come from Canada, or You (formal) come from Canada
why: sie (they) and Sie (formal you) share the infinitive form: kommen. She would be sie kommt.

q: Which sentence is right?
why: heute takes the first place, so the verb comes second and ich follows it.

q: In Am Montag habe ich Zeit, what is the first element?
why: Am Montag is one building block, so habe is in second place.

q: Does aber count as the first element?
o: No: aber joins two sentences and takes no place
why: aber and und take no place: …, aber morgen arbeite ich.

q: What does wer mean?
why: wer means who. Where is wo.

q: How do you ask Do you live in Berlin? (to a friend)
why: No do in German: the verb simply comes first, with its du ending.

q: Which word asks where someone is going?
why: wohin asks where to; woher asks where from; wo asks where.

q: What time is halb vier?
why: halb looks ahead to the next hour: half way to four, so 3:30.

q: How do you say 42?
why: Ones before tens, joined with und: zweiundvierzig.

q: How do you say €2.50?
why: Euros, the word Euro without -s, then the cents.

q: Which forms of fahren take the umlaut?
o: Only du and er, sie, es
why: Stem changes happen only with du and er, sie, es: du fährst, er fährt.

q: What are you having? (to a friend)
why: nehmen changes to nimm- in the du form: nimmst.

q: I'm going to Hamburg =
why: ich keeps the normal stem: ich fahre.

q: 'I'm looking for a sweater' (der Pullover) =
why: Pullover is masculine and the direct object, so ein becomes einen.

q: What happens to die Jacke when it is the direct object?
why: Only masculine articles change in the accusative; feminine die stays die.

q: Den Rock kauft Anna. Who is buying?
why: den marks Rock as the direct object, so Anna is the subject, even though she comes last.

q: 'I don't have a car' =
why: Before a noun that would take ein, use kein; Auto is neuter, so kein has no ending.

q: How do you say 'That's not expensive'?
why: nicht goes right before an adjective, and kein is only for nouns.

q: 'I don't have an appointment' (der Termin) =
why: Termin is masculine and the direct object, so kein becomes keinen.

q: 'Anna and her brother' =
why: The owner is Anna, so ihr; Bruder is masculine and the subject, so no ending.

q: 'I'm visiting my brother' =
why: Bruder is masculine and the direct object, so mein becomes meinen.

q: Who is being asked in Wie ist Ihr Name?
why: Ihr with a capital I means your (formal). With a small i, ihr Name would be her name or their name.

q: 'I like playing tennis' =
why: For an activity, use the verb + gern, with the verb second.

q: 'I like dogs' =
why: For animals, things and people, use mögen: ich mag. Ich möchte Hunde would mean you want some dogs.

q: What does Am liebsten trinke ich Tee mean?
o: Most of all, I like to drink tea.
why: am liebsten means most of all; the verb trinke still comes second.

q: 'I can speak German' =
why: Sentence bracket: kann in second place, the infinitive sprechen at the end.

q: What does Ich will Deutsch lernen mean?
why: will is a form of wollen: it means want, not the future.

q: What does Ich muss heute nicht arbeiten mean?
o: I don't have to work today.
why: muss nicht means don't have to. Must not is darf nicht.

q: 'I get up at seven' =
why: aufstehen is separable: stehe in second place, auf at the end.

q: Which verb does NOT separate?
why: ver- is an inseparable prefix, so verstehen always stays in one piece.

q: 'I have to get up early' =
why: After a modal, the separable verb is the infinitive at the end, in one piece.

q: 'I'd like to go to Berlin' =
why: Sentence bracket: möchte second, fahren last, nach Berlin in the middle.

q: 'When does the train arrive?' (ankommen) =
why: kommt follows wann, and the prefix an closes the bracket at the end.

q: In the sentence bracket, what goes at the very end?
o: The second verb part: an infinitive or a separable prefix
why: The conjugated verb is second; the infinitive or the separable prefix comes last.

q: 'I'm going by bus' (der Bus) =
why: mit always takes the dative, and masculine der becomes dem.

q: 'I'm going to the pharmacy' (die Apotheke) =
why: zu + a shop; feminine die becomes der in the dative, and zu der becomes zur.

q: Which one means 'I'm going home'?
why: nach Hause means going home; zu Hause means at home.

q: How do you say I'm cold (you feel cold)?
why: Feeling cold uses the dative: Mir ist kalt. Ich bin kalt describes your personality.

q: That's for you. (to a friend)
why: für always takes the accusative, and the accusative of du is dich.

q: Can you help me? (to a friend)
why: helfen takes the dative, mir, and the infinitive goes to the end.

q: I'm going to the movies.
why: Where to? in takes the accusative: ins Kino (in das Kino).

q: on Monday
why: Days take am: am Montag.

q: I've lived in Berlin for two years (and still do).
why: seit with the present tense: the living started two years ago and is still going on.

q: Call me, please! (formal)
why: Sie imperative: the infinitive first, then Sie; the separable prefix an goes to the end.

q: Take a pill! (to a friend)
why: du nimmst without -st and without du: Nimm!

q: Drive carefully! (to a friend)
why: du fährst drops the umlaut in the imperative: Fahr!

q: I went to Berlin (by train).
why: Moving from A to B takes sein, and the participle gefahren goes to the end.

q: Which is the past participle of verstehen?
why: Verbs with the inseparable prefix ver- take no ge-: verstanden.

q: I ate pizza.
why: essen takes haben, and the participle gegessen goes to the end.

q: Where were you? (to a friend)
why: The du form of war ends in -st: warst.

q: We had no time.
why: The wir form is hatten. Adding gehabt makes it we had had time.

q: That's true.
why: true is wahr, with an h; war means was.

q: The sweater is expensive.
why: After sein the adjective has no ending; teurer would mean more expensive.

q: cheaper than
why: Add -er to the adjective, and than is als.

q: My brother is older than me.
why: alt adds an umlaut in the comparative: älter als.

q: If I have time, I'll come.
why: After wenn the verb goes to the end, and the main verb comes right after the comma.

q: I'm staying home because I'm sick. (use denn)
why: denn does not change the order: ich bin krank.

q: Which word sends the verb to the end?
why: wenn sends the verb to the end; aber, oder and denn leave the order alone.

q: What does Ich bekomme ein Geschenk mean?
why: bekommen means get, and a present is ein Geschenk; das Gift is poison.

q: Your friend says: Ich will nach Hause. What does she mean?
why: will is a form of wollen, so it means want.

q: I'm hot. (how you feel)
why: How you feel takes mir: Mir ist heiß. Ich bin heiß means something else.
